title: Ethiopia Launches Offline AI Teacher Assistant in National Push, Backed by World Bank
excerpt: . Ethiopia Launches Offline AI Teacher Assistant in National Push, Backed by World Bank. Amanuel Kindeya. October 27, 2026. New tool runs on standard laptops without internet, as Ethiopia expands AI in classrooms from teacher coaching to vocational training. Ethiopia has launched a pilot AI teaching assistant that works entirely offline on standard laptops, the latest step in a national effort to bring artificial intelligence into classrooms with World Bank support. The "Agentic AI Teacher Assistant" is built on grades 9–12 textbooks and can generate lesson plans and exam questions. The Ministry of Education launched the pilot in mid-October 2026, positioning it as a practical response to the country's connectivity constraints. The tool falls under the World Bank-funded Ethiopia Education Transformation Operation for Learning (ETOL) project, which has total financing of approximately 226 million US dollars from the World Bank and partners including the UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, the Global Partnership for Education, Finland, Norway, and UNICEF. Within ETOL, the World Bank's IDA commitment stands at 50 million US dollars, alongside a 46. 37 million US dollars Global Partnership for Education Fund contribution. The new assistant follows an earlier "AI-Coach" pilot with more than 350 English and mathematics teachers. That tool runs as an app on teachers' existing phones and keeps working even when the internet goes down. Teachers in the pilot said its feedback was timely, relevant to their lessons, and easy to use in class. At the World Bank's Human Capital Ministerial Conclave on October 19, 2026, National Bank Governor Eyob Tekalign (PhD) presented AI Coaches and AI Tutors in secondary schools as part of Ethiopia's wider skills agenda. He also pointed to a new collaboration with the World Bank on an AI-enabled skills platform for technical and vocational training that is designed to be gender-responsive. Ethiopia's digital education plans, set out in Digital Ethiopia 2030 and its National AI Policy, have run into deep-rooted obstacles that predate the current AI push. The education system faces severe foundational challenges. According to the World Bank, 90 percent of ten-year-olds in Ethiopia cannot read a simple sentence. Many teachers do not pass their licensing exams, and those who do enter classrooms that are overcrowded and short of basic materials. Insufficient training opportunities are a critical challenge, with one mathematics teacher describing the shortage as a defining obstacle. The country ranks in the 10th percentile globally on education futures readiness. Teacher technological knowledge scores remain low, even as recognition of technology's usefulness stays high. ICT education remains in its early stages, constrained by limited infrastructure, a shortage of qualified teachers, and poor internet connectivity. In public schools, formal ICT instruction begins only in grade 7, leaving significant gaps in earlier grades. A study of Ethiopian educators found that AI integration into the K-12 curriculum remains limited despite growing policy attention. Teachers have also expressed concerns specific to digital tools. Research on technology adoption in Ethiopian schools identifies inadequate infrastructure, high costs, and insufficient teacher training as substantial barriers, alongside socio-cultural factors such as stigma and social exclusion. At the higher education level, a continental survey of Ethiopian respondents identified funding shortfalls and unsatisfactory pay or incentives as the most severe constraints on digital and AI adoption, each scoring 4. 5 on a five-point scale. Flawed management models ranked next at 4. 3, followed by insufficient infrastructure and inadequate professional development support, both at 4. 2. Backbase Launches Delivery Factory with AI Agents for Banks
excerpt: Share LinkedIn Facebook Twitter Copy Link Telegram Email. Free Newsletter. Get the hottest Fintech Singapore News once a month in your Inbox. Backbase has launched Delivery Factory, an AI-powered software development platform that enables banking delivery teams to work alongside specialised AI agents. Teams using the platform across more than 10 Backbase implementations over the past 12 months delivered projects twice as fast as traditional teams and 30% faster than those using generic AI coding assistants. Backbase also reported an 80% reduction in effort spent on requirements and specifications, 40% less coding and review effort, and a 60% increase in test and automation coverage. Unlike general-purpose coding assistants, Delivery Factory combines project requirements, architecture specifications, meeting notes and Backbase product knowledge into a shared context. This allows development teams and AI agents to work from the same information throughout design, planning, implementation and review, reducing the need to repeat requirements at each stage. The platform includes a Business Analyst Agent that generates specifications, user stories and acceptance criteria for Jira work items. A Solution Architect Agent supports technical design decisions, while separate Backend, Mobile and Web Agents prepare implementation plans based on project requirements and the bank’s Backbase version. Engineers retain oversight of code changes and verification results, while delivery leads coordinate project scope and planning. “Delivery Factory gives them and their AI agents a shared foundation: what the bank has agreed on, how its project is designed and how Backbase works,”. said Greg Fahy, CTO Digital Banking at Backbase. The company has also introduced two additional AI agents to support platform migration and upgrades. The Backbase Migration Agent helps banks move existing customer journeys, integrations and business logic to its Banking OS platform without rebuilding them from scratch. Meanwhile, the Backbase Upgrade Agent helps existing customers apply platform changes and identify areas requiring attention, making upgrades part of ongoing development rather than separate projects. title: Bankenwahl: Die neue Macht der KI-Empfehlungen
summary: Generative KI-Systeme wie ChatGPT unterstützen Kunden nicht nur bei der Informationssuche. Sie treffen auch eine erste Vorauswahl, etwa bei der Suche nach einer neuen Bank. Das verändert den Wettbewerb.
excerpt: Leben & Karriere. Fintech. Mediathek. English News. Middle East. Asia. Advertorials. Newsletter. Über uns. Werbung. Suche. Dienstag, 27. Oktober 2026. KOLUMNE Bankenwahl: Die neue Macht der KI-Empfehlungen. Generative KI-Systeme wie ChatGPT unterstützen Kunden nicht nur bei der Informationssuche. Sie treffen auch eine erste Vorauswahl, etwa bei der Suche nach einer neuen Bank. Das verändert den Wettbewerb. Andy Dreckmann, Senior Kommunikationsberater bei der Zürcher Kommunikationsagentur C-Factor. (Bild: zVg). Dienstag, 27. Oktober 2026 10:13. Bankenwahl: Die neue Macht der KI-Empfehlungen. Von Andy Dreckmann. Jemand fragt ChatGPT: «Ich bin 52 Jahre alt, selbstständig und habe ein Vermögen von rund 2 Millionen Franken. Ich suche im Raum Zürich eine Bank für Anlagen, Vorsorge, Pensionierung und Nachlass. Nachhaltigkeit ist mir wichtig. Welche Banken kommen infrage?». Die KI nennt zwei oder drei Institute und begründet ihre Auswahl. Für die nicht genannten Banken entsteht ein neues Risiko: Potenzielle Kund:innen beschäftigen sich möglicherweise gar nicht erst mit ihnen. KI-Empfehlungen haben reale Konsequenzen. Eine Similarweb-Studie aus den USA zeigt: Wer von ChatGPT eine Marke empfohlen bekam, besuchte deren Website im Durchschnitt 2,5-mal häufiger als die eines direkten Wettbewerbers. Eine KI-Empfehlung ist also mehr als nur eine neue Form der Markenpräsenz. Sie kann mitbestimmen, mit welchen Anbietern sich potenzielle Kund:innen anschliessend überhaupt noch beschäftigen. Genau deshalb ist diese Vorauswahl durch KI-Systeme so relevant. Bei jeder Kundenfrage entsteht eine neue Vorauswahl. Für die Schweiz liefert der IFZ AI Visibility Banking Report der Hochschule Luzern konkrete Hinweise. Bei allgemeinen Fragen dominieren bekannte Institute wie die UBS, Raiffeisen und die ZKB. Werden die Kundenbedürfnisse spezifischer, kann sich die Auswahl jedoch deutlich verändern. Die Alternative Bank Schweiz wird bei allgemeinen Bankfragen kaum genannt. Bei Fragen nach nachhaltigen Banken rückt sie dagegen bei allen drei getesteten KI-Systemen stark in den Vordergrund. Dabei verweisen die KI-Antworten unter anderem auf ein WWF-Rating und weitere externe Quellen. Die Schlussfolgerung lautet: Es gibt nicht die eine KI-Vorauswahl relevanter Banken. Sie entsteht je nach Kundenfrage neu und Markenstärke allein garantiert keine KI-Empfehlung. Auch kleinere Banken können bei spezifischen Bedürfnissen punkten, wenn ihre Positionierung klar und glaubwürdig extern belegt ist. Warum Webanalytics den KI-Einfluss oft nicht zeigen. Der direkte Traffic aus KI-Systemen ist aktuell meist noch gering. Daraus zu schliessen, dass sie kaum relevant sind, wäre jedoch verfrüht. Denn wie Similarweb zeigt: Viele Nutzer:innen wechseln nach einer KI-Empfehlung nicht direkt zur Website der empfohlenen Marke. 55,9 Prozent der späteren Besuche erfolgten über eine Suchmaschine. Nur 8,8 Prozent führten direkt über einen KI-Kanal auf die Website. Die Webanalyse sieht also häufig Google als Quelle. Dabei bleibt unsichtbar, dass die Entscheidung, nach dieser Bank zu suchen, bereits früher beeinflusst worden sein kann. KI verändert damit womöglich weniger den letzten messbaren Kontakt als den Schritt davor. Was KI-Systeme über eine Bank wissen. Damit stellt sich die strategische Frage: Nach welchen Kriterien entscheidet ein KI-System, welche Banken es in einer bestimmten Situation empfiehlt? Die eigene Website ist hierfür nur ein Teil des Bildes. Eine AirOps-Untersuchung zu kommerziellen KI-Anfragen zeigt: 85 Prozent der analysierten Markennennungen wurden Drittquellen zugeordnet. Das beweist zwar keine Kausalität. Es zeigt aber, wie präsent externe Informationen in KI-Antworten sind. Das digitale Markenbild entsteht also nicht allein aus der eigenen Kommunikation, sondern auch aus Medien, Vergleichsportalen, Ratings, Studien und Bewertungen. Die entscheidende Frage lautet daher nicht nur: Was sagen wir über uns selbst? Sondern auch: Findet sich dieses Bild im digitalen Raum

title: Bank scam warning signs: How to spot fake texts, emails and AI-powered scams
excerpt: Bank scam warning signs: How to spot fake texts, emails and AI-powered scams. 'Banks Never Ask That' campaign is revamped to address latest scam tactics. Prev Next. Learn the red flags to spot fake messages about your bank account. By: Alicia Smith. Posted 1:08 PM, Oct 26, 2026. SOUTHFIELD, Mich. (WXYZ) — A text or email warns of suspicious activity on your bank account. It looks legitimate, and the urge to click can be immediate. But that message could be coming from a scammer — not your bank. The American Bankers Association’s “Banks Never Ask That” campaign aims to help consumers recognize those traps as criminals use increasingly convincing texts, emails, websites and even artificial intelligence to impersonate trusted companies. See the full story from Alicia Smith in the video below. Bank scam warning signs. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watching after the ad Visit Advertiser website GO TO PAGE. “It really is a big issue,” said Paul Benda, Executive Vice President for Risk, Fraud and Cybersecurity at the American Bankers Association. Consumers describe suspicious messages and links. Asked whether he receives texts claiming to be from his bank, Detroit resident Brandon Jackson said, “Most of the time I ignore them. ”. Domenique Wood, who was visiting metro Detroit from New Jersey, said she has accidentally clicked suspicious links. “Yeah, literally, all the time [including] at work sometimes which is really bad,” she said with a laugh. Gautam Bogg, visiting from Philadelphia, said the prevalence of scam attempts did not surprise him. “Maybe not so surprised because they’ve probably gotten smarter over the past couple of years,” Bogg said. AI makes impersonation harder to spot. Benda said consumers cannot rely only on familiar warning signs such as strange wording or typos. Criminals are using AI to make fraudulent websites and emails resemble communications from banks and other trusted companies. He added that they also use deepfakes to imitate someone’s voice or face. “The criminals are leveraging AI just like we are. And so, they've gotten much more advanced,” Benda explained. Benda pointed to a joint study by Gallup and the Stop Scams Alliance on 2025 financial scams. He said the study estimated that scammers stole $68 billion from Americans — roughly $186 million a day — affecting about 15 million U. S. adults. He said the findings also showed that 12% of successful scams in 2025 involved artificial intelligence or deepfakes. Where to learn the warning signs. The American Bankers Association recently updated its “Banks Never Ask That” campaign with scam tactics and resources to help consumers protect their financial information. The website covers five major categories:. Email scams. Text scams. Phone scams. AI and deepfake scams. Payment app scams. Consumers can take the site’s Scam Slayer Quiz to test their ability to recognize suspicious messages. The site also offers guidance on scam warning signs and strengthening an online bank account, along with reminders to hang up, delete suspicious messages and block scam contacts. Resources are also available to educate people about check fraud. Learn more at BanksNeverAskThat. com. excerpt: . Kamana Sewa Bank launches digital AI assistant “KS Mitra”. Onlinekhabar Tuesday, October 27, 2026. 0 Comments. Shares. Kamana Sewa Bikas Bank has launched KS Mitra, an AI-based customer support and complaint management system, with the aim of providing customers with faster, easier and more effective service. The bank said customers can make account inquiries, banking requests and complaint-related queries through the “Ask Mitra” icon available on the bank’s official website, by email at ksmitra@kamanasewabank. com , or directly through WhatsApp at 9851460085. Through KS Mitra, customers can get information about the bank’s services, get account-related information and lodge complaints without visiting a branch. The bank said customers can easily find the bank’s branches and contact numbers, its services and facilities, interest rates, service charges and other general information. According to the bank, once the customer’s identity and account details are verified, they can also obtain information including account balance, transaction details, outstanding loan amount, CRN, demat and KYC details. Services such as blocking an account, changing the source of income or occupation, changing the mobile banking password or PIN, blocking mobile banking and checking its status will also be provided. “If the information a customer seeks is not available through this, a ticket will be issued automatically, making it easier to follow up on and resolve the customer’s queries, service requests and complaints,” the bank said. The bank said the facility is a new and impactful digital dimension in Nepal’s banking sector.
